title: Two Translations, One Poem: Hear the Choices
subtitle: An additional Daily Read: A five-minute way to read translations as creative work—and give translators their due.
imageAlt: Two women sit together at a table, each holding a different English edition of the same poem and comparing a marked line.
imageConcept: Two women friends with distinct builds and features sit side by side at a sunlit table, each holding a different published English translation of the same poem. One points to a line on her page while the other listens, with both books’ translator credits visible; the mood is curious, not competitive.
body: A poem can change in one word

Read a poem in two English translations and you may meet two different kinds of attention. One version might feel spare; another might make an image seem closer, stranger or more musical. The useful question is not which one is “right.” It is what each version asks you to notice.

Translation is often treated as a transparent passage from one language to another, as though the translator’s task were to carry over an unchanged object. But choices about sound, rhythm, word meaning and line breaks shape what a poem becomes for readers in English. In a discussion of translating Halina Poświatowska, Karolina Zapal and Ryan Mihaly describe weighing sound as well as meaning; one example is their consideration of “autocrat” and “ruler,” words that can point toward similar authority but carry different tones in English [1].

That kind of decision is not a flaw to catch. It is a way into the work. A small comparison gives readers something concrete to hear without pretending that an English-language response can settle every question about the original.
Not a contest, and not a test

A comparison can slide quickly into a verdict: one translation is faithful, the other is loose; one is beautiful, the other is plain. Those judgments can be tempting, but they may claim more than a reader can know from English alone. You can notice how two versions affect you without claiming expertise in the source language or deciding what the poem must mean.

There may not be one definitive translation that makes all other versions unnecessary. Mira Rosenthal’s essay on translation addresses this absence of a single “correct” or “definitive” version [2]. That does not mean every choice is interchangeable. It means that reading can begin with attention rather than a winner’s podium: What does this word bring forward? What does that line break slow down? What feeling arrives in one version that the other leaves quieter?

Keeping the exercise open is especially helpful when readers have different tastes. In reporting on the 2026 PEN Poetry in Translation Award, Julia Goldberg describes judges bringing different preferences to their conversations and considering accessibility, aesthetic experience and the work of evaluating translations [3]. Disagreement, then, need not signal that someone has failed to understand. It can show how a poem offers more than one point of entry.

Choose a short poem available in two published English translations. A library, a translated poetry collection or a literary publication can be a good place to look. Check that each version identifies its translator; if you are unsure whether two texts are translations of the same poem, confirm that in the book or publication rather than relying on a similar title.

Read both versions aloud if that is comfortable for everyone. If not, read silently. Start with the first version and let it sit for a moment; then read the second. There is no need to explain the poem before you begin, look up every unfamiliar reference or agree on an interpretation. The point is to have two distinct encounters with the words.

Then each person chooses one difference. It could be a single word, an image, a line break, punctuation, a repeated sound or the pace of a sentence. Take turns saying what that choice made you notice. A useful prompt is, “In this version, I hear or picture…” That keeps the observation grounded in the page and leaves room for another reader’s response.

Vague comparisons can leave readers with little to discuss: “I liked this one more,” or “That one felt more poetic.” Those reactions are welcome, but give them a detail to lean on. Instead of “the first is stronger,” try: “The shorter word makes the line sound abrupt to me,” or “The break makes me pause before the image.” You are describing an effect, not issuing a ruling.

Listen for sound even when the meaning seems clear. Does a phrase move quickly or make you slow down? Is there a repeated consonant, a strong beat, or an awkwardness that seems deliberate? Notice whether one translation uses a familiar word while another feels formal or unusual. The example of “autocrat” and “ruler” is useful precisely because a choice can preserve a broad idea while shifting its register and sound [1].

Lineation matters, too. A phrase at the end of a line can feel suspended; the same phrase carried into the next line may feel more conversational. Punctuation can make a voice seem certain, hesitant or interrupted. These are not secret codes with one answer. They are features readers can point to and then test against their own experience of the poem.

After comparing, look for a translator’s note, introduction or afterword. It may explain a difficulty, describe an approach or offer context for a choice. Read it as an invitation into the translator’s thinking, not as an answer key that invalidates your response. Your first impression still matters; the note adds another kind of information.

If the publication does not include a note, the reading is not incomplete. You can still name what you observed and acknowledge what you do not know. Readers do not need fluency in the source language to notice how English words, rhythms and images land. At the same time, awareness of that limit keeps personal response distinct from claims about the original poem or the translator’s intentions.

A good discussion can hold both things at once: “This image felt vivid to me” and “I can’t tell from this version alone what the translator had to weigh.” That combination is not hedging. It is a way to take the poem seriously without treating a reader’s reaction as the whole story.
Put the translator’s name in the conversation

When you talk about a translated poem, name the poet and the translator or translators. Instead of saying only “I read a poem by…,” try “I read [poet] in a translation by [translator].” Credit can also include the edition or publication if you are sharing the poem with someone who wants to find it.

This small habit responds to a larger visibility problem. PEN America judge Alta L. Price says translators are often erased and that some reviewers neglect to mention them [3]. The reader cannot fix how publishing credits are displayed, but can refuse to repeat the omission in ordinary conversation. A translator’s name belongs with the work, not in the fine print of a reading experience.

If there are two translators, name both. If you are sharing a passage, use the credited edition and follow its rules for quotation; a short discussion does not require reproducing the poem. You can simply describe the word or line break that caught your attention and point someone toward the book.

This exercise works with a partner, a small group or one reader keeping two notes on the page. People can pass on reading aloud or on explaining a response. A language background, a poetry vocabulary or a confident opinion is not a prerequisite. The only essential materials are two credited translations and a willingness to be specific about what you notice.

For a closing question, ask what each version made newly visible. Maybe one brought forward a sound, while another made an image easier to picture. Perhaps the difference is small, or perhaps it changes the poem’s mood for you. You do not have to resolve that tension before moving on.

The next time you encounter a translated poem, take a moment to find the translator’s name and read a few lines with that person’s choices in mind. Not as a test of fidelity, and not as a hunt for a perfect version: just as an invitation to hear how literature travels, and who helped it arrive.
